name: live_spiral
conclusions: Design limitation: on all 6 contested questions both modes read the same set of passages (k=3 per hop, 4 hops, no re-reading, a corpus of 8), so the corpus is exhausted and guarded cannot change which evidence is seen. The balance loss comparison is not informative here. In 16 of 16 runs the final hop retrieved nothing, so a counter-query fired at the hop before it has no effect on what is read.

Balance loss here is |sum of ground-truth stances / number of passages|, with neutral passages counted in the denominator. The Research tab uses (supporting - contradicting) / (supporting + contradicting) on the model's own stances, so the two are not comparable.
Contested, balance loss at last non-empty hop (ground truth): standard 0.167, guarded 0.167, change +0.000: not informative, the corpus is exhausted in both modes.
Contested, balance loss averaged over all hops: standard 0.315, guarded 0.315, change +0.000: not informative, the corpus is exhausted in both modes.
Contested, mean BAQD at hops 2 to 4 (hops that read no passages are left out): standard -0.102, guarded -0.106, change -0.004: no meaningful difference.

Settled control: every passage supports, so balance loss near 1.0 is correct. Standard 1.000, guarded 1.000, mean CQI firings per guarded run 3.00. Guarded did not distort settled evidence, but this is trivially true when every passage supports and all of them are read.

The guard fired 3.0 times per run on settled questions, where the evidence is one-sided because the claim is true. So the skew trigger has false positives: it cannot tell settled evidence from biased retrieval.
Mean BAQD for the standard agent is below zero (-0.102), so the live model does not clearly bend its queries toward its belief on this metric.

Home charging at off-peak tariffs cuts energy cost per kilometre well below petrol, with savings growing as distance rises [ev_cost#2]. Fleet data reports electric vehicles reducing fuel spending by 60 percent per kilometre and producing clear five-year running savings [ev_cost#0]. Electric drivetrains need fewer serviced parts, so scheduled servicing costs fall [ev_cost#1], and purchase incentives and road tax exemptions can lower the effective price in most markets [ev_cost#3]. Without home charging, public rapid charging can approach petrol cost per kilowatt hour, eroding the advantage [ev_cost#7].

runs.one_line: Daily vitamin D helps mainly deficient adults; routine use in adequate-level adults shows no clear outcome benefit and high doses carry risks.
runs.answer: The passages give a mixed picture, so a blanket daily recommendation for all adults is not clearly supported. Supplementation reliably corrects deficiency and improves bone mineral density in adults with low baseline serum levels, which supports daily use in that group [vitamin_d#0]. Deficient populations also show better muscle strength and fall rates after daily supplementation [vitamin_d#3]. A meta-analysis reports a modest fracture benefit in older adults when vitamin D is combined with calcium [vitamin_d#1]. In contrast, a Cochrane review found no reduction in all-cause mortality in adults who are not deficient at baseline [vitamin_d#5], and the VITAL trial found no significant effect on cardiovascular events or cancer [vitamin_d#4]. Routine supplementation in adequate-level populations showed no measurable outcome improvement and adds cost and pill burden [vitamin_d#6]. High doses have been linked to hypercalcaemia and, in some trials, to increased fall risk [vitamin_d#7]. Observational links to fewer infections are associational only [vitamin_d#2]. Overall, daily use seems most justified for deficient adults.

runs.question: does remote work increase employee productivity

hops.query: does remote work increase employee productivity
hops.belief: Remote work appears to modestly increase employee productivity in some settings, such as call centres and via lower turnover, but evidence is mixed and self-reports may overstate gains.

hops.query: meta-analysis remote work productivity objective output versus self-reported studies
hops.belief: Remote work appears to modestly increase productivity for some roles, such as individual deep-work and call centre jobs, but team-level effects are mixed or negative and the evidence is uncertain.

hops.belief: Remote work's effect on productivity is mixed and role-dependent: it may modestly raise output for some knowledge or deep-work roles but can lower it for routine or team-based tasks.

runs.one_line: Remote work's productivity effect is mixed: gains in some call-centre and engineering settings, losses in data entry and team mentoring.
runs.answer: The evidence is mixed rather than uniform. A randomised call centre experiment found a 13 percent increase in completed calls among remote staff, attributed to a quieter environment and fewer breaks [remote_work#0]. Output per engineer measured by completed tickets held steady or improved after full transitions to distributed work in several large technology firms [remote_work#3]. Remote arrangements also reduce attrition, and lower turnover limits productivity losses from repeated hiring and retraining [remote_work#2]. Against this, a large field experiment found remote data entry workers were 18 percent less productive than office counterparts on identical tasks [remote_work#6]. Studies of software teams report slower onboarding and weaker mentoring for juniors, which can depress team output over time [remote_work#4]. Communication also becomes more siloed after a remote transition [remote_work#5]. Self-reported productivity gains often fail to appear in objective output measures [remote_work#7], so self-report evidence should be discounted.

runs.one_line: Evidence is mixed: competitive models predict job losses, but many studies find near-zero employment effects, with some negative local results.
runs.answer: The passages do not give a single verdict. Standard competitive models predict that a binding wage floor above equilibrium reduces labour demanded and so causes job losses [min_wage#0]. Some regional studies found falls in teen and low-skill employment after sharp increases [min_wage#3], and studies of large local rises report reduced scheduled hours for low-wage workers [min_wage#1]. Employers in low-margin sectors may also automate, cutting entry-level positions [min_wage#2]. Other evidence points the other way: the Card and Krueger fast food study found no employment decline in New Jersey [min_wage#4], monopsony models suggest a moderate floor can raise both wages and employment [min_wage#5], and a meta-analysis finds effects clustered near zero, with publication bias inflating negative findings [min_wage#6]. Some observed firms kept headcount broadly unchanged because lower turnover offset labour costs [min_wage#7]. On balance, the evidence suggests employment effects are small on average but can be negative in some settings, depending on the size of the increase and labour market structure.

runs.one_line: Fasting produces weight loss mainly via calorie deficit; it shows no clear advantage over standard calorie restriction when intake is matched.
runs.answer: The passages suggest intermittent fasting can produce weight loss, but mainly through a calorie deficit rather than meal timing itself. Time restricted eating reduced total daily energy intake for many participants, producing weight loss over twelve week trials [fasting#0]. Some participants found an eating window easier to follow than continuous restriction, and reduced evening snacking helped account for part of the deficit [fasting#1][fasting#3]. However, head to head trials matching total calories found no weight loss advantage over continuous restriction across twelve months [fasting#4]. Benefits in short trials largely disappeared once total energy intake was controlled [fasting#7]. Dropout rates in fasting arms also exceeded those in standard restriction arms in several studies, undermining claims of superior long term adherence [fasting#6]. Overall, the evidence supports fasting as a route to weight loss only insofar as it creates an energy deficit.

runs.one_line: Nuclear is low-carbon and firm, but slow, costly and unresolved on waste, so it is a partial solution.
runs.answer: The passages suggest nuclear power has real strengths for cutting carbon emissions but also serious drawbacks, so it is a partial rather than a clear-cut solution. On the positive side, lifecycle emissions per unit of nuclear electricity are comparable to wind and lower than solar [nuclear#0], and its firm output independent of weather could reduce the storage a decarbonised grid would need [nuclear#1]. Its land use is also far lower than wind or solar per unit of energy [nuclear#3], and countries with large nuclear fleets decarbonised their grids faster than those relying on renewables alone over the same period [nuclear#2]. On the negative side, construction takes a decade or more, so new plants may not cut emissions within near-term climate windows [nuclear#5]. Recent projects have run late and over budget, leaving nuclear costs uncompetitive with renewables in some cases [nuclear#4], and cost overruns have pushed some utilities into severe distress [nuclear#7]. Long-term waste disposal also remains unresolved, as no country has yet commissioned a large permanent high-level waste repository [nuclear#6].

runs.answer: Nuclear power has real strengths as a low-carbon option. Its lifecycle emissions per unit of electricity are comparable to wind and lower than solar, making it one of the lowest-carbon sources available [nuclear#0]. Its firm, weather-independent output could reduce the storage a decarbonised grid would otherwise need [nuclear#1], and countries with large existing nuclear fleets decarbonised their grids faster than comparable countries relying on renewables alone [nuclear#2]. Waste disposal also remains unresolved, as no country has commissioned a permanent high-level waste repository at scale [nuclear#6]. On balance, nuclear is a strong low-carbon option for the long term, but its speed and cost are serious drawbacks, so confidence in it as a universal solution is moderate.

runs.answer: Yes, the passages support smoking as a cause of lung cancer. Major public health authorities classify tobacco smoking as an established cause of lung cancer based on the full weight of accumulated evidence [smoking#6]. Cohort studies show lung cancer incidence rising steeply with cumulative cigarette exposure in a clear dose response relationship [smoking#0]. Risk declines after cessation, with the size of the decline tracking years since quitting, which supports causation over confounding [smoking#3]. Case control studies across many countries and decades report consistent and large effect sizes [smoking#4]. Tobacco smoke contains identified carcinogens that form DNA adducts in bronchial epithelium, giving a biological mechanism for tumour initiation [smoking#1]. Animal experiments reproduce airway tumours [smoking#5], and population lung cancer rates fall after sustained declines in smoking [smoking#2]. Second hand smoke also raises risk in non smokers [smoking#7].

runs.answer: Yes, the passages support a causal link between smoking and lung cancer. Major public health authorities classify tobacco smoking as an established cause of lung cancer based on the full weight of accumulated evidence [smoking#6]. Cohort studies following millions of participants show lung cancer incidence rising steeply with cumulative cigarette exposure in a clear dose response relationship [smoking#0]. Case control studies across many countries and decades report consistent and large effect sizes [smoking#4]. Risk declines progressively after cessation, with the size of the decline tracking years since quitting, which supports causation over confounding [smoking#3]. Lung cancer rates fall in populations after sustained declines in smoking prevalence [smoking#2]. Tobacco smoke contains carcinogens that form DNA adducts in bronchial epithelium, providing a biological mechanism [smoking#1]. Animal experiments reproduce airway tumours [smoking#5]. Second-hand smoke also raises risk in non-smokers [smoking#7]. No contradicting passages were provided, so this conclusion rests on uniformly supportive evidence.

runs.answer: Yes, the passages indicate that measles vaccines prevent measles infection. Two doses of a measles-containing vaccine give about 97 percent protection against infection in controlled effectiveness studies [vaccines_measles#0]. Serological studies show neutralising antibodies persisting for decades after the standard two-dose schedule [vaccines_measles#3]. At the population level, national incidence fell by more than 99 percent after routine childhood vaccination was introduced [vaccines_measles#1], and outbreaks concentrate among unvaccinated people [vaccines_measles#2]. Resurgence follows declines in coverage [vaccines_measles#7]. Post-exposure vaccination within 72 hours reduces the probability of clinical disease [vaccines_measles#6]. The passages support protection, though they do not address vaccine failure rates in detail beyond the roughly 97 percent figure.

design_limitation: Design limitation: on all 6 contested questions both modes read the same set of passages (k=3 per hop, 4 hops, no re-reading, a corpus of 8), so the corpus is exhausted and guarded cannot change which evidence is seen.
